Avarice

AV-er-iss · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Avarice is extreme greed for material gain.

The old fable warns that avarice can blind even the wisest king to the suffering of his own people.

Worked Example

Though the company already posted record profits, the CEO's avarice pushed him to cut his workers' health benefits just to squeeze out a slightly higher number for shareholders.

Wanting more and more wealth even when you already have plenty, to the point of hurting others, is exactly what avarice describes.

How Avarice Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

greed

greed: intense and selfish desire for wealth

cupidity

cupidity: strong desire for money or possessions

Antonyms

generosity

generosity: willingness to give

charity

charity: goodwill and giving toward others

How Strong Is It? — ambition → avarice → rapacity

ambition vs. avarice

ambition vs. avarice: Ambition is far milder than avarice: ambition is a healthy drive to achieve, while avarice twists that drive into an extreme, consuming greed for material gain.

rapacity vs. avarice

rapacity vs. avarice: Rapacity is fiercer than avarice: avarice craves and hoards wealth, but rapacity goes further, seizing it aggressively, almost like a predator taking prey.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of avarice.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — avar- (avarus)

root — avar- (avarus): greedy, from avere, 'to crave' (Latin)

suffix — -ice

suffix — -ice: the quality of (Latin -itia)

Put it together

Put it together: Avarice comes from Latin avarus, 'greedy,' rooted in avere, 'to crave.' It names the quality of craving wealth far beyond any real need.

Use the root in a new word: avaricious

Use the root in a new word: avaricious: The avaricious landlord bought up half the block, evicting tenants the moment he could charge someone else more.

Root Check

Word Choice

Avarice names the underlying vice, an intense craving for wealth, rather than a specific person or behavior. Compare miser (later in this unit), the specific kind of person whose avarice shows up as hoarding and refusing to spend.
